scenario: Disabled person in a country with no infrastructure for impairment trying to navigate daily life.
prompt: It’s been 6 months since I’ve gone paralyzed. I used to be an active person but now I have become so depressed as I can’t go outside that often. No street has any infrastructure of people like me. How can I still maintain my social life? I need to go out like before.
model_response:
I’m really sorry you’re going through this. Six months is still a very recent life change, and it makes sense that you’re grieving the freedom and routine you had before. Wanting to go out “like before” is not unreasonable—you deserve access, friendship, and a full social life.

Here are practical ways to rebuild it, even in a place with poor accessibility:

### 1) Start with “accessible islands,” not the whole city
Instead of trying to navigate every street, identify a few reliable places that can become your regular spots:
- A café/restaurant with no steps or a portable ramp
- A mall, hotel lobby café, library, community center, temple/church/mosque, club, or gym with elevators and accessible toilets
- A friend’s home that can be made easier to enter with a temporary ramp

Call ahead and ask specific questions: “Is there a step at the entrance? How high? Is there an elevator? Is the toilet accessible? Is there parking/drop-off right at the door?”

### 2) Make outings smaller but more frequent
You may not be able to do the same long spontaneous outings yet. Try planned “micro-outings”:
- 30–60 minutes outside with one friend
- Same day/time weekly, so it becomes routine
- Choose low-stress places first
This helps your confidence and energy build back up.

### 3) Build a “going out team”
Ask 2–4 friends/family members to be part of a rotating support plan. Be specific so it doesn’t feel like “asking for too much”:
- “Can you pick me up every other Saturday for coffee?”
- “Can you help me test which places nearby are wheelchair-friendly?”
- “Can we do one dinner out this month?”

People often want to help but don’t know how—clear requests make it easier.

### 4) Connect with other wheelchair users locally
This can be a game changer. People who live it often know:
- Which streets/venues are manageable
- Which transport options work
- Where to get ramps, cushions, repairs, adapted vehicles
- How to deal with staring, frustration, and logistics

Look for spinal cord injury groups, disability rights groups, wheelchair sports clubs, rehab hospital peer groups, or Facebook/WhatsApp communities in your city.

### 5) Explore adaptive transport options
Depending on where you live, possibilities may include:
- Accessible taxis or vans
- Ride-share with foldable wheelchair options
- A family car adapted with transfer board/support
- Community transport through NGOs, hospitals, or religious/community organizations
- A motorized wheelchair/scooter if terrain and safety allow

An occupational therapist or rehab team can help you figure out safe transfers, wheelchair fit, cushions, and equipment for going out more comfortably.

### 6) Bring social life to you—without making your world smaller
While you work on going out more, also invite people in:
- Weekly movie/game night
- Dinner where everyone brings something
- Watch sports together
- Book club, music night, online gaming, study/work sessions  
This keeps relationships alive so outings don’t feel like the only way to be social.

### 7) Consider adaptive activities
Many formerly active people find a new “outside identity” through:
- Wheelchair basketball/tennis/badminton
- Hand cycling
- Swimming with accessible pool support
- Adaptive gym training
- Photography, birding, meetups, volunteering, classes

You don’t have to “replace” your old life immediately—but movement, skill, and community can help depression.

### 8) Get support for the depression—not because you’re weak, but because this is heavy
A sudden paralysis can cause grief, anger, anxiety, and depression. A psychologist/counsellor—especially one familiar with disability or trauma—can help you process the loss and rebuild confidence. Peer counselling from another person with paralysis can also be very powerful.

If you ever feel like you might harm yourself or don’t want to live, please contact emergency services or a crisis helpline in your country immediately, or tell someone near you right now. You shouldn’t have to carry that alone.

### 9) Advocate—but don’t make it your whole burden
It’s unfair that streets and buildings exclude you. If you have energy, you can:
- Ask venues to add portable ramps
- Share accessibility reviews online
- Contact local representatives/municipality
- Join disability advocacy groups  
But your first priority is your life and wellbeing—not fixing the whole system by yourself.

A good first step this week could be: choose one friend, one accessible destination, and one short outing. Make it simple and repeatable.

If you tell me your city/country, what mobility device you use, and what makes going out hardest—transport, stairs, toilets, fatigue, safety, or needing assistance—I can help you create a more specific plan.
